write.desc: This topic extends the Riemann integral to unbounded intervals and unbounded functions by taking limits of ordinary integrals, develops tests for when those limits exist, and uses the comparison between sums and integrals to prove the integral test for series.

points.name: Improper integrals over an unbounded interval
points.what: Define the integral of f from a to infinity as the limit of the integral from a to b as b tends to infinity, for f integrable on every [a,b], and say precisely what convergence and divergence mean. Understand that this is a limit of ordinary Riemann integrals, not a new kind of integral, and that changing the lower endpoint a does not affect convergence.
outside: definition of the Riemann integral of a bounded function on a closed bounded interval via upper and lower Darboux sums
limit of a function as x tends to infinity (epsilon-M definition)
additivity of the Riemann integral over adjacent intervals

points.name: Improper integrals of functions unbounded near an endpoint
points.what: Define the integral of f over (a,b] as the limit of the integral over [c,b] as c tends to a from the right, when f is integrable on each [c,b] but may be unbounded near a. Recognise that this is the same idea as point 1 applied to a one-sided limit at a finite endpoint.
outside: definition of the Riemann integral of a bounded function on a closed bounded interval via upper and lower Darboux sums

points.name: Integrals improper at both ends or at interior points
points.what: Handle integrals such as the integral over the whole real line or over (0, infinity) by splitting at an interior point into separate improper integrals that must each converge, and prove the answer does not depend on the split point. Contrast this with the symmetric limit (Cauchy principal value), using f(x) = x on the real line as an example where the symmetric limit exists but the integral diverges.
outside: additivity of the Riemann integral over adjacent intervals

points.name: The p-integrals: 1/x^p on [1, infinity) and on (0,1]
points.what: Prove that the integral of 1/x^p from 1 to infinity converges exactly when p > 1 and the integral from 0 to 1 converges exactly when p < 1, with p = 1 diverging at both ends, by computing the integrals over [1,b] and [c,1] and taking limits. These are the standard benchmarks for every later comparison.
outside: fundamental theorem of calculus: the integral of F' over [a,b] equals F(b) - F(a)

points.name: Nonnegative integrands: convergent if and only if bounded
points.what: Prove that when f is nonnegative, the function b -> integral from a to b of f is increasing, so the improper integral converges exactly when these integrals are bounded, and then equals their supremum. This is the improper-integral version of the monotone convergence theorem and the basis of the comparison tests.
outside: an increasing function bounded above has a limit at infinity equal to its supremum (least upper bound property)

points.name: Comparison and limit comparison tests for improper integrals
points.what: Prove that if 0 <= f <= g, convergence of the integral of g implies convergence of the integral of f and divergence of f implies divergence of g, and the limit comparison form when f/g has a positive finite limit. Use them with the p-integrals to decide convergence of integrals such as 1/(1+x^2), e^(-x^2) or 1/sqrt(x(1+x)).

points.name: Cauchy criterion for improper integrals
points.what: State and prove that the integral of f from a to infinity converges if and only if for every epsilon > 0 there is M such that the integral from b to b' of f has absolute value less than epsilon whenever M <= b < b'. Note that, unlike for series, convergence of the integral does not force f(x) to tend to 0.
outside: Cauchy sequences of real numbers converge (completeness)

points.name: Absolute convergence implies convergence
points.what: Define absolute convergence of an improper integral and prove that it implies convergence, either through the bound 0 <= f + |f| <= 2|f| and the comparison test or through the Cauchy criterion. Understand that the converse fails, which makes conditional convergence possible.
outside: integrability of |f| and the triangle inequality for integrals

points.name: sin(x)/x: a conditionally convergent integral
points.what: Prove that the integral of sin(x)/x from 1 (or 0) to infinity converges, by integrating by parts to reduce it to the absolutely convergent integral of cos(x)/x^2, and that the integral of |sin(x)|/x diverges, by bounding it below on each interval [k pi, (k+1) pi] by a multiple of 1/(k+1) and comparing with the harmonic series.
outside: integration by parts as a theorem with hypotheses

points.name: The integral test for series
points.what: For f positive and decreasing on [1, infinity), prove that the sum of f(k) converges if and only if the integral of f from 1 to infinity converges, by showing that on the partition of [1,n] into unit intervals the lower and upper Darboux sums are f(2)+...+f(n) and f(1)+...+f(n-1), which gives the inequalities linking partial sums and integrals. Know exactly where positivity and monotonicity are used.
outside: a series of nonnegative terms converges if and only if its partial sums are bounded
upper and lower Darboux sums of a function on a partition

points.name: p-series by the integral test
points.what: Apply the integral test with f(x) = 1/x^p to prove that the sum of 1/n^p converges exactly when p > 1, and apply it to series such as the sum of 1/(n ln n) and 1/(n (ln n)^2). Recognise this as a second proof of the p-series result, alongside the one by comparison or Cauchy condensation.

points.name: Estimating the tail of a series with integrals
points.what: Prove that for f positive and decreasing the tail sum of f(k) for k > n lies between the integral of f from n+1 to infinity and the integral from n to infinity, and use this to bound the error of a partial sum, for example to find how many terms of the sum of 1/n^2 give a chosen accuracy.

points.name: Sum minus integral: Euler's constant
points.what: Prove that for f positive and decreasing the sequence f(1)+...+f(n) minus the integral of f from 1 to n is decreasing and bounded below, so it converges; with f(x) = 1/x this gives Euler's constant and shows that the n-th harmonic number grows like ln n.
outside: the natural logarithm as the integral of 1/t from 1 to x

points.name: Why the integral test needs a decreasing function
points.what: Give examples showing that without monotonicity the series and the integral can behave differently: a nonnegative continuous function made of ever narrower spikes whose integral converges although f(n) does not tend to 0, and f(x) = sin^2(pi x), whose series is 0 while its integral diverges. This shows the integral test is a theorem with a hypothesis, not a recipe.
